Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that enables large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and incorporate new information from external data sources [1]. It modifies interactions with an LLM so that the model responds to user queries by referring to a specified set of documents, supplementing its pre-existing training data [1][3].

This approach allows LLMs to use domain-specific and updated information without needing frequent retraining [1][3]. By pulling relevant text from databases, uploaded documents, or web sources before generating responses, RAG helps reduce AI hallucinations and stick to the facts [1][3].

The data that RAG references is typically converted into LLM embeddings, which are numerical representations in a large vector space, and these embeddings are stored in a vector database for document retrieval [1]. 

In practical terms, such as in the office model of RAG, data is prepared by the Chopper character, who cuts long texts into small pieces called chunks [3]. These chunks are then turned into fingerprints or vectors by the Translator, capturing what the text means so they can be compared with user questions [4].

Hybrid vector approaches combine dense vector representations with sparse one-hot vectors [1]. This allows them to take advantage of the computational efficiency of sparse dot products over dense vector operations [1].
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can be used on unstructured, semi-structured, or structured data [1]. Examples of structured data include knowledge graphs [1].

A vector database, vector store, or vector search engine is a database that stores and retrieves embeddings in vector space, and typically implements approximate nearest neighbor algorithms [1].

Generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs) are a type of large language model that is pre-trained to predict the next word [1][2]. They use only the decoder part of the transformer architecture and are pre-trained to predict the next token in a sequence [3].

Project Treble is a major re-architecture of the Android OS framework introduced by Google in May 2017 with the announcement of Android 8.0 [1][3]. It is designed to make updating devices to newer versions of Android easier, faster, and less costly for manufacturers [1].

Treble achieves this by separating the vendor implementation from the Android OS framework using a new "vendor interface" [1]. This stable vendor interface provides access to hardware-specific parts, enabling device makers to deliver new Android releases simply by updating the framework without requiring additional work from silicon manufacturers [1].

Semantic search is a search method that focuses on meaning, aiming to improve accuracy by understanding the searcher's intent and the contextual meaning of terms [1]. Modern systems achieve this by using vector embeddings that convert words, phrases, or documents into numerical vectors to find results based on meaning [1].

In contrast, lexical search is an approach where the search engine looks for literal matches of the query words or variants of them [1]. It operates without understanding the overall meaning of the query [1].

Deepfakes are images, videos, or audio that have been generated or edited using artificial intelligence, audio-video editing software, or AI-based tools [1]. They can depict either real or fictional individuals [1].

This technology is considered a form of synthetic media, which is typically created by artificial intelligence systems that combine various media elements into a brand-new media artifact [1]. The term is a portmanteau combining "deep learning" and "fake" [1].

Algorithmic bias refers to a systematic and repeatable harmful tendency in a computerized sociotechnical system to produce unfair outcomes [1][2]. This can include privileging one category or arbitrary group over another in ways that may differ from or align with the algorithm's intended function [1][2]. 

This type of bias involves algorithms that reflect systematic and unfair discrimination, which can impact areas ranging from privacy violations to the reinforcement of social biases related to race, gender, sexuality, and ethnicity [1]. It can emerge from intentional design choices, technical limitations, or the unintended use and collection of data to train algorithms [1][3].

Prompt engineering is the process of structuring natural language inputs, known as prompts, in order to produce specified outputs from a generative AI model [1]. It can also be defined as the practice of designing and refining these input instructions to make outputs more accurate, relevant, or useful [1].

According to the Oxford English Dictionary, it is the action or process of formulating and refining prompts for an artificial intelligence program or algorithm to optimize its output or achieve a desired outcome [2]. The discipline involves understanding how a model interprets language and may utilize techniques such as few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought prompting, and role assignment [1].

An AI hallucination is a response generated by artificial intelligence that presents false or misleading information as fact [1]. These responses may include plausible-sounding random falsehoods, such as fabricated citations [1]. 

The term has also been characterized by various organizations and sources in the context of large language models as inventing facts during uncertainty, making logical mistakes, fabricating information while behaving as if stating facts, and producing misleading or nonsensical factual errors [4].

The project switched from Rive to GSAP because of two main problems [1][2]. First, the coding assistant helping to build the project cannot edit Rive files, meaning every single change would have had to go through Kenneth in the Rive editor [1][2]. Second, Rive files can only switch between scenes that are drawn in advance, whereas this project needs to draw real data such as one card per real chunk [1][2]. 

To test a better way, Kenneth ran a spike where he built the Upload cycle and the Ask cycle in GSAP on a flat SVG [2]. Because it worked, ADR 004 replaced the Rive plan on 9 October [2].
